claims.claim: The data plane kept operating during the March 26 power failure, while Analytics remained impaired.
claims.rationale: The report explicitly separates the unaffected data plane from Analytics, which was not fully restored until later that day.

claims.claim: All customer-facing functions returned to normal by 15:05, including Analytics.
claims.rationale: APIs and dashboards were normal at 15:05, but Analytics recovered later. The claim incorrectly extends the earlier recovery to every function.

claims.claim: The March 26 Analytics interruption affected more than 1,000 customers.
claims.rationale: The full report describes Analytics impairment and affected users without a customer count. The number remains unknown.

claims.claim: The initial assessment identified overly restrictive breaker settings as a contributor, without establishing when those settings were configured.
claims.rationale: The assessment identifies incorrect breaker coordination as one contributor and explicitly says the configuration date is unknown; it is not a final exclusive-cause claim.

claims.claim: The report establishes when the breaker settings involved in the March 26 failure were configured.
claims.rationale: The report explicitly says it does not know when those settings were established.

claims.claim: The same engineer configured the breaker settings on all four switchboards.
claims.rationale: The full report names neither a responsible engineer nor who configured each board. A common operator is not established.

claims.claim: Automatic API and dashboard recovery preceded full Analytics restoration.
claims.rationale: APIs and dashboards recovered without human intervention within seven minutes, while Analytics returned later that day.

claims.claim: Every service recovered without manual intervention after the March 26 power loss.
claims.rationale: The report explicitly identifies a few services requiring human intervention and subsequent work to automate them.

claims.claim: Analytics was fully restored at exactly 21:30 UTC on March 26.
claims.rationale: Later that day supplies ordering, not an exact Analytics restoration timestamp. The full report does not establish 21:30.

claims.claim: The June 20 incidents increased both HTTP errors and high-percentile response latency.
claims.rationale: The introduction and impact description report elevated HTTP errors and almost threefold p99 time to first byte.

claims.claim: Every HTTP request handled by Cloudflare failed during the June 20 incidents.
claims.rationale: The report gives partial error percentages, explicitly far below every request. Higher latency also affected requests without making all requests fail.

claims.claim: More than 10,000 distinct customers experienced the June 20 incidents.
claims.rationale: The full report describes a significant set of customers and request error percentages, without a distinct customer count.

claims.claim: A new DDoS rule exposed a latent rate-limit bug, while backbone congestion was a separate event.
claims.rationale: The report distinguishes the two events and says the new rule worked as expected but exposed existing rate-limit logic under particular cookie inputs.

claims.claim: The two cookie-validation functions always agreed, so their disagreement could not trigger the infinite loop.
claims.rationale: The report explicitly says these functions can disagree for mixed valid and invalid cookies; that disagreement drives self-recursion and a nonterminating CPU loop.

claims.claim: A single identified customer sent every request that poisoned a process during the June 20 incident.
claims.rationale: The full report explains the request condition and its redistribution but identifies neither one customer nor a sole request source.

claims.claim: Restarting poisoned processes restored capacity, while redirecting the triggering requests could spread the failure to other servers.
claims.rationale: Restarts helped recover affected service. Rerouting did not repair poisoned processes and carried triggering requests to other servers.

claims.claim: Traffic Manager kept issuing new routing actions throughout 18:35–18:52 UTC.
claims.rationale: The report explicitly identifies this interval as one in which Traffic Manager issued no new routing actions because its own exception handling halted activity.

claims.claim: Exactly 5,000 servers received a service restart during recovery.
claims.rationale: The report describes widening and rolling restarts without a total server count. The full text does not establish this exact total.

claims.claim: Some affected requests reached Cloudflare with high latency, while others were blackholed before reaching its servers.
claims.rationale: The report distinguishes unreachability from successful but slow delivery, including later leaked paths with high latency.

claims.claim: All affected users lost reachability throughout the DNS incident, with no successful requests reaching Cloudflare.
claims.rationale: The report explicitly describes requests reaching Cloudflare at high latency during the incident, contradicting universal uninterrupted unreachability.

claims.claim: The DNS incident caused more than one million dollars in customer losses.
claims.rationale: The full report describes network and user reachability impact but supplies no monetary-loss assessment.

claims.claim: The leaked /24 route had a valid RPKI origin even though its propagation path was invalid.
claims.rationale: The report explicitly separates valid origin validation for AS13335 from an invalid AS path caused by the route leak.

claims.claim: The invalid /32 updates appearing in Cloudflare BMP data prove that Cloudflare accepted those routes for forwarding.
claims.rationale: The report labels those updates pre-policy and explicitly states that Cloudflare rejected them on import. Observation in BMP is not acceptance.

claims.claim: AS267613 intentionally originated the /32 route to disrupt Cloudflare.
claims.rationale: The full report identifies the origin and invalid route but does not establish the operator intent. Its background explicitly allows accidental or purposeful hijacks.

claims.claim: The /32 blackholing appeared resolved while the /24 leak still added latency, before the leak was fully resolved at 02:28 on June 28.
claims.rationale: The 22:16 timeline entry distinguishes apparent hijack resolution from continuing leaked-route latency; final leak resolution comes later.

claims.claim: Disabling the first partner peering at 20:08 resolved all impact, with no further route leaks or high latency.
claims.rationale: Later leaked paths, high latency and additional peer shutdowns explicitly continue after the first action. Complete resolution was not immediate.

claims.claim: Exactly 100,000 requests experienced high latency after 22:16 UTC.
claims.rationale: The full report describes continuing high latency and final resolution without this request total or a count for the interval.

source_cautions: Same-assistant controlled claims and references after full source inspection, before any new Jev outcome. No independent reference review.
Discovery search exposed content before allocation, including substantial DNS text; source selection was not blinded.
Whole retrospective reports include causal hindsight, prior incidents and future proposals. Text excludes images but retains prose, lists, tables and code.
June 20 timeline says 19:34 for full DDoS-rule disablement; later prose says 19:36. Claims avoid asserting either precise disablement time without changing the source.
Publisher and longer whole-report context change together; effects cannot be attributed solely to either factor.
These public reports may be in model pretraining. Claims are controlled study text, not authentic analyst entries.
